dek: Anaplan let big companies plan the whole business in one live model instead of a thousand spreadsheets.
lede: Anaplan's engine held a company's entire plan in memory, so one changed assumption flowed through every number in seconds. That speed was the pitch. Big companies planned in thousands of disconnected spreadsheets, and Anaplan let finance, sales and supply chain teams work from one live model. When it filed to go public in 2018, cloud software was the market's favorite category. Investors paid rich prices for any subscription business with steady growth and loyal enterprise customers.

sections.heading: A Calculation Engine from Yorkshire
sections.body: Anaplan began in Yorkshire, England, where Guy Haddleton and Michael Gould built a new calculation engine for business models. Gould had worked on planning software before. He thought the older tools were too slow and too rigid. Their engine held huge models in memory, so a change in one assumption could flow through the whole plan in seconds. The company later moved its headquarters to San Francisco to be closer to customers and capital.

sections.heading: A Fight Over Employee Pay
sections.body: Anaplan priced its shares at $17 in October 2018, and the stock jumped on its first day of trading. Revenue kept climbing over the next few years. Losses stayed large. In 2022 Thoma Bravo agreed to buy the company. Then the two sides fought over employee pay, and the price was trimmed to about $10.4 billion. Anaplan became a private company again.

cover.artwork: Plan of Chicago, Chicago, Illinois, Diagram Showing City Growth

tagline: A Chef's Recipes, Then Everyone's Logs
dek: Elastic gave developers a free, fast way to search mountains of text, logs and security data.
lede: Elasticsearch started as a way for Shay Banon's wife to search her recipes. By 2018 it ran inside thousands of companies, often before anyone in purchasing knew it was there. Developers used the free, open source engine to search huge piles of text, logs and events in near real time. Elastic, the company behind it, sold support, hosted services and extra features on top. Its public offering tested whether that open source model could carry a large public company.

sections.heading: Free Software as the Bait
sections.body: Shay Banon began writing search software while building a recipe search tool for his wife, who was training as a chef. He released Elasticsearch as open source in 2010, and developers passed it around fast. In 2012 Banon and his co-founders formed a company around it. Their bet came in two halves. Free software would win the users. Companies that ran it at scale would then pay for help running it.

sections.heading: Fencing Out the Cloud Giants
sections.body: Elastic priced at $36 a share in October 2018, and the stock nearly doubled on its first day. Growth kept coming as logs, security and observability became its main markets. Cloud providers had started to offer Elasticsearch as their own service. Elastic changed its license to stop them. The company remains public, with its headquarters split between the Netherlands and California, and trades on the New York Stock Exchange.

dek: Upwork let businesses hire skilled freelancers anywhere in the world, with contracts and payment handled for them.
lede: Upwork began as two rivals, Elance and oDesk, that merged and became the largest online market for freelance work. A business posted a job. Freelancers around the world sent proposals. Upwork handled the contract and the payment. When the company went public in 2018, many people already earned part of their income working remotely. Stephane Kasriel, chief executive since 2015, took the combined company to the market as the biggest name in the field.

sections.heading: Work Without the Building
sections.body: Elance and oDesk started from the same idea: skilled work does not need to happen in the client's building. Elance launched in 1999. oDesk followed a few years later with tools that tracked remote work hours. The two rivals merged in 2013 and took the name Upwork in 2015. The combined company bet that trust, payments and reviews in one place would keep both sides coming back.

sections.heading: Remote Work Goes Normal
sections.body: Upwork priced its shares at $15 in October 2018 and opened well above that price. Over the following years it shifted toward larger business clients and higher fees. Then the 2020 pandemic made remote work normal, and the marketplace drew new attention. Upwork remains a public company and one of the best known names in freelance work. Its shares trade on Nasdaq under the ticker UPWK.

cover.theme: a carpenter at his bench (work for hire)

fate: Renamed Momentive; taken private by STG, 2023 ($1.5B)
dek: SurveyMonkey let anyone write a survey, send a link and watch the answers come back in charts.
lede: SurveyMonkey grew for a decade with almost no outside money, and its name became a generic word for an online poll. Anyone with a browser could build a survey, send a link and watch the answers arrive. Students, small businesses and Fortune 500 companies all used it. The company filed as SVMK Inc. in 2018, after years as one of Silicon Valley's best known private companies. It hoped to prove that a freemium tool could also sell to large enterprises.

sections.heading: Ten Years Without Investors
sections.body: Ryan Finley started SurveyMonkey in 1999 as a simple tool for building online surveys. His brother Chris joined him, and the two grew the company for ten years with almost no outside money. Investors bought it in 2009. Dave Goldberg led it from then until his death in 2015. The bet was that millions of small paying users could carry a large, durable software business.

sections.heading: A Merger Shareholders Refused
sections.body: SVMK priced at $12 a share in September 2018 and jumped on its first day. Zander Lurie was chief executive. In 2021 the company renamed itself Momentive Global to stress its enterprise products. A planned merger with Zendesk then fell apart after shareholders objected. In 2023 the private equity firm STG bought the company for about $1.5 billion and took it private.

dek: Eventbrite let anyone running an event, from a yoga class to a conference, sell tickets online.
lede: Eventbrite gave a yoga teacher the same box office as a conference planner. Organizers set up a page, sold tickets and checked guests in at the door, and Eventbrite took a small fee on each ticket. It filed to go public in 2018, after a decade of steady growth and its recent purchase of Ticketfly, a ticketing company for music venues. Live events were booming. Eventbrite served the long tail of small organizers.

sections.heading: Ticketing Beyond the Arena
sections.body: Julia Hartz, Kevin Hartz and Renaud Visage started Eventbrite in 2006. Back then a few large companies controlled ticketing, and they served arenas. Neighborhood venues were left out. The founders bet that the internet made it possible to serve millions of small events with the same software. Julia Hartz later became chief executive, and she led the company through its public offering.

sections.heading: When the Events Stopped
sections.body: Eventbrite priced at $23 a share in September 2018 and jumped on its first day. Then the 2020 pandemic halted live events. The business took a hard hit, and the company cut staff to survive. It rebuilt slowly as events returned. In late 2025 the Italian software group Bending Spoons agreed to buy Eventbrite for about $500 million in cash. The deal closed in 2026.

cover.artwork: Fireworks at Ryogoku (Ryogoku hanabi), from the series "One Hundred Famous Views of Edo (Meisho Edo hyakkei)"

fate: Taken private by Vista Equity Partners, 2022 ($8.4B)
dek: Avalara worked out the sales tax on every sale and filed the returns, so businesses did not have to.
lede: Avalara went public in June 2018, and days later the Supreme Court made its product essential. The company automated one of the dullest, most painful jobs in commerce. A business that sold in many places had to track thousands of sales tax rates and rules. Avalara's software looked up the right tax for each sale, filed the returns and kept the records. The court's Wayfair case would decide whether states could tax online sellers with no local presence.

sections.heading: Tax Software on Bainbridge Island
sections.body: Avalara began in 2004 as a small team on Bainbridge Island, near Seattle. Scott McFarlane and his co-founders saw that sales tax software was mostly built for large companies, and it was hard to use. They bet that a cloud service could plug into shopping carts and accounting tools and do the work for a business of any size. Every new tax rule made the service more valuable.

sections.heading: South Dakota v. Wayfair
sections.body: Avalara priced at $24 a share in June 2018. Days later the Supreme Court decided South Dakota v. Wayfair. The ruling let states require online sellers to collect sales tax, even with no local presence. Many more businesses suddenly needed what Avalara sold, and the stock climbed for years. In 2022 Vista Equity Partners bought the company for about $8.4 billion and took it private.

tagline: A Loan on the Contractor's Phone
dek: GreenSky let contractors and medical offices offer customers instant loans, funded by partner banks.
lede: A homeowner buying a new roof or kitchen could apply for a loan on the contractor's phone and get a decision in seconds. That was GreenSky. Partner banks funded the loans, and GreenSky ran the technology and collected fees. When it filed to go public in 2018, fintech lenders were popular with investors. GreenSky was one of the most profitable among them, and it kept the loans off its own books.

sections.heading: Leave the Lending to Banks
sections.body: David Zalik founded GreenSky in Atlanta in 2006. He had already built and sold a software business. He saw home improvement contractors losing sales when customers could not pay up front. His bet was to give merchants a simple financing tool and leave the lending itself to banks. That kept the loans off GreenSky's books, so the company could grow fast with little capital.

sections.heading: Below the Offering Price
sections.body: GreenSky priced at $23 a share in May 2018, and the stock fell soon after. Investors worried about rising funding costs and the company's reliance on a few bank partners. Shares traded far below the offering price for most of its public life. In 2022 Goldman Sachs bought GreenSky for about $2.2 billion to grow its consumer lending business. The next year Goldman agreed to sell it.

cover.theme: an open spring sky over the river
cover.artwork: Fishing in Spring, the Pont de Clichy (Asnières)

fate: Taken private by Vista Equity Partners, 2021 ($3.5B)
dek: Pluralsight taught developers and IT staff new technical skills through a library of expert video courses.
lede: Pluralsight started with four trainers teaching developers in person, then moved the whole business online. By 2018 its library held thousands of video courses on programming languages, cloud platforms and security, taught by working experts. Companies bought seats for their engineering teams to keep up with fast-changing tools. When Pluralsight filed to go public that year, every business was becoming a software business. The shortage of skilled developers was a common complaint.

sections.heading: Four Trainers Go Online
sections.body: Aaron Skonnard and three fellow trainers started Pluralsight in 2004 as a classroom training company. Teaching developers in person was costly and hard to scale. In 2008 they moved the whole business online and began recording courses. Their bet was that a large catalog of expert video, sold by subscription, could reach far more learners than any classroom. The company was based in Farmington, Utah.

sections.heading: Skill Scores, Then a Buyout
sections.body: Pluralsight priced at $15 a share in May 2018 and rose on its first day. It grew its business sales and added skill assessments and analytics for managers. Then growth slowed, and the stock never held its early highs. Aaron Skonnard ran the company as chief executive through all its public years. In 2021 Vista Equity Partners bought Pluralsight for about $3.5 billion and took it private.

cover.theme: a scholar reading in a hut (learning)

dek: Dropbox put your files on every computer and phone you owned, and made sharing them easy.
lede: Dropbox exists because Drew Houston forgot his USB drive on a bus trip. His fix was a special folder. Put a document in it, and the document appeared on every other computer and phone you used. That simple trick won hundreds of millions of users, most of them on free plans. When Dropbox filed to go public in 2018, it was one of the largest private tech companies of its era. The question was whether enough of those users would pay.

sections.heading: A Demo Video, a Waitlist
sections.body: Houston started Dropbox in 2007. He and Arash Ferdowsi joined Y Combinator and built a product that hid all the hard parts of keeping files in sync. A short demo video spread widely and filled a waiting list. Their bet was simple. People would love a free product, and enough of them would pay for more space to build a real business.

sections.heading: Leaving Amazon's Cloud
sections.body: Dropbox priced at $21 a share in March 2018, above its expected range, and the stock jumped on its first day. Before the offering, it had moved most of its storage off Amazon's cloud and onto its own servers to cut costs. In later years growth slowed as rivals bundled storage with other software. Dropbox remains a public company, still led by Drew Houston.

cover.artwork: Sudden Shower over Shin Ohashi Bridge and Atake (Ohashi Atake no yudachi), from the series "One Hundred Famous Views of Edo (Meisho Edo hyakkei)"

tagline: Owning the Wires Behind the Apps
dek: Bandwidth gave software companies phone numbers, calling, texting and 911 service through simple code.
lede: Bandwidth's customers came to include Microsoft, Google and Zoom, yet most people who used its network never saw its name. It sells the plumbing behind modern calling and texting. Software companies use its APIs to place calls, send messages and connect emergency 911 service. When it filed to go public in 2017, cloud communications was a crowded field. Bandwidth stood apart because it owned much of its own nationwide network.

sections.heading: Raleigh, Without Much Venture Money
sections.body: David Morken and Henry Kaestner started the company in North Carolina in 1999, first selling internet connections. Over time they built a voice network and won large customers that needed reliable phone service inside their software. Their bet was that owning the network, instead of renting it, would bring better quality and lower costs. The company stayed in Raleigh and grew without much venture money.

sections.heading: Buying a European Carrier
sections.body: Bandwidth priced at $20 a share in November 2017. It grew as video meetings, contact centers and messaging apps moved to the cloud. In 2020 it bought Voxbone, a European carrier, to expand overseas. Demand surged during the pandemic, as so much of life moved onto calls, and later cooled. Bandwidth remains a public company in Raleigh, and David Morken stayed on as chief executive.

tagline: What Is Plugged In Right Now
dek: Forescout showed companies every device on their network and kept risky ones away from everything else.
lede: Many big networks could not answer a basic question: what is plugged in right now. Forescout could. Its software spotted laptops, phones, printers, cameras and factory machines as they joined, without an agent installed on any of them. Then it applied rules to block or isolate the risky ones. When Forescout filed to go public in 2017, internet-connected devices were multiplying in offices, hospitals and plants, and few companies knew how many they had.

sections.heading: Researchers from Israel
sections.body: Forescout was founded in Israel in 2000 by a group of researchers and engineers led by Professor Hezy Yeshurun. Its early product focused on stopping network attacks. Over time it shifted toward visibility. The thinking was plain: a company cannot protect devices it does not know about. Forescout later moved its headquarters to San Jose, California, and kept its research in Tel Aviv.

sections.heading: A Buyout Fought Over
sections.body: Forescout priced at $22 a share in October 2017. It grew by selling to large enterprises and government agencies, and to hospitals and factories, where unmanaged devices were a growing worry. In 2020 Advent International agreed to buy the company. The two sides fought over the deal during the pandemic, then settled on a lower price. Forescout became private later that year.

dek: Roku made streaming on the TV easy, first with small boxes, then with software built into sets.
lede: Roku means six in Japanese, because it was the sixth company Anthony Wood had started. Its small boxes and sticks plugged into a TV and showed apps from Netflix, Hulu and hundreds of others. Later, TV makers built Roku's software right into their sets. When Roku filed to go public in 2017, cord cutting was well underway. The company was starting to earn more from advertising and platform fees than from hardware.

sections.heading: A Box Built With Netflix
sections.body: Anthony Wood founded Roku in 2002. He had already invented an early digital video recorder. Roku's first streaming box arrived in 2008, built with Netflix. The bet was that a neutral home screen would win viewers. Roku would sit between the viewer and every streaming service and favor none of them. Owning that screen would be worth more than selling the devices.

sections.heading: Ads on the Home Screen
sections.body: Roku priced at $14 a share in September 2017 and soared on its first day of trading. During the streaming boom of 2020 the stock rose many times over, then fell back. The company kept adding active accounts and building its ad business. Its software now runs inside many of the TV sets sold in the United States. Roku remains public, still led by its founder.

cover.theme: a river print from a series of six (roku means six)
cover.artwork: No. 6: Tama River of Koyasan in Kii Province, from the series "Six Jewel Rivers of the Floating World (Ukiyo Mu Tamagawa)"

dek: Redfin let people buy and sell homes with salaried agents, honest data and lower commissions.
lede: Redfin paid its real estate agents a salary and asked customers to review them, in an industry built on commissions. Its website showed listings with maps and data, and its own agents worked with people buying and selling for lower fees. Most brokerages treated software as an afterthought. When Redfin filed to go public in 2017, the housing market was strong. Redfin was one of the few online brokerages that had lasted.

sections.heading: From Map Site to Brokerage
sections.body: David Eraker and Michael Dougherty started Redfin in Seattle in 2004 as a map-based home search site. Glenn Kelman joined as chief executive soon after and turned it into a full brokerage. He led the company for about two decades. The bet was that customers wanted honest data and lower costs, and that salaried, reviewed employees would serve them better than independent agents chasing commissions.

sections.heading: Rising Rates, Then Rocket
sections.body: Redfin priced at $15 a share in July 2017 and rose on its first day. It later tried buying and reselling homes itself, then shut that business in 2022 as interest rates rose. The housing slowdown hit revenue and the stock. In 2025 Rocket Companies, the mortgage lender, bought Redfin in an all-stock deal valued at about $1.75 billion. The Redfin brand lives on under Rocket.

dek: Tintri made storage that understood virtual machines, so IT teams could tune each application on its own.
lede: Tintri filed for bankruptcy about a year after it went public. The company built storage hardware for the age of virtual machines. Older systems thought in disks and volumes. Tintri's systems understood each virtual machine, so administrators could see and tune performance one application at a time. By the time Tintri filed to go public in 2017, storage was moving fast toward flash and cloud services, and its rivals were larger, with deep pockets.

sections.heading: A VMware Veteran's Fix
sections.body: Kieran Harty, a former VMware engineering leader, founded Tintri in 2008 with a small team of storage engineers. Virtualization had changed how data centers worked, and storage had not caught up. Their bet was that storage designed around virtual machines would be simpler to run and faster to fix. Tintri raised large venture rounds and won hundreds of enterprise customers.

sections.heading: Twelve Months to Bankruptcy
sections.body: Tintri cut its price range and priced at $7 a share in June 2017, well below its early hopes. The stock fell soon after. Losses were heavy, competition grew and cash ran short. For a company that had raised so much venture money, the fall came fast. In July 2018, about a year after its offering, Tintri filed for bankruptcy. DataDirect Networks bought its main assets and kept the product alive.

dek: Blue Apron shipped measured ingredients and recipe cards so people could cook dinner at home without shopping.
lede: Blue Apron went public in the same month Amazon agreed to buy Whole Foods, and investors suddenly worried about competition in food. The company mailed dinner. Each week a box arrived with fresh ingredients in exact amounts and illustrated recipe cards. Customers cooked the meal themselves and skipped the grocery store. When Blue Apron filed to go public in June 2017, it led a wave of meal kit startups.

sections.heading: A Chef's Supply Chain
sections.body: Matt Salzberg, Ilia Papas and Matt Wadiak started Blue Apron in New York in 2012. Wadiak was a chef. The founders wanted to make cooking at home easier and less wasteful. They built their own warehouses and supply chain to buy food directly from farms. Their bet was that a subscription would keep customers cooking week after week and answer the daily question of dinner.

sections.heading: Customers Cancel, Wonder Buys
sections.body: Blue Apron cut its price range and priced at $10 a share in late June 2017. The stock fell steadily as customers canceled and marketing costs stayed high. The company did a reverse stock split and changed leaders several times. In 2023 Wonder Group, the food hall and delivery startup, bought Blue Apron for about $103 million. Blue Apron kept selling meal kits under Wonder.

cover.theme: a cook and his wife (home cooking)

dek: Carvana let people buy a used car online, finance it and have it delivered to their door.
lede: Carvana sold used cars out of coin-operated glass vending towers. Buyers browsed photos, arranged financing and signed papers online. Then they had the car delivered or picked it up from a tower. A seven-day return policy replaced the test drive. When Carvana filed to go public in 2017, nearly all used cars still changed hands at traditional lots. Few people believed buyers would skip the test drive.

sections.heading: Born Inside DriveTime
sections.body: Carvana started in 2012 inside DriveTime, a used car dealer run by the Garcia family in Arizona. Ernie Garcia III, Ryan Keeton and Ben Huston built it as a separate online business. Their bet was that software could replace the worst parts of buying a car, the haggling and the paperwork. The car vending machine became the symbol of that idea.

sections.heading: Near the Edge and Back
sections.body: Carvana priced at $15 a share in April 2017 and fell on its first day. Then the stock rose many times over as sales grew. In 2022 it bought the physical sites of ADESA's auction business. High rates and heavy debt pushed the company near the edge, and the stock collapsed. Carvana restructured its debt, returned to profit and recovered. It remains public.

dek: Presidio designed, installed and ran the networks, data centers, cloud systems and security of midsize companies.
lede: Presidio made much of its money reselling equipment from partners such as Cisco, then wrapping its own engineers around the boxes. Those engineers designed networks, installed data center gear, moved workloads to the cloud and managed security. The customers were midsize companies across the United States. When Presidio filed to go public in 2017, it was a large but quiet business. Apollo, the private equity firm, had bought it two years earlier.

sections.heading: Built From Regional Firms
sections.body: Presidio grew by buying regional IT service firms. The private equity firm Apollo bought the company in 2015 and prepared it for a public offering. The bet was that midsize businesses needed one trusted partner to handle complex technology. The shift to cloud and security would create steady demand for skilled engineers. Presidio's engineers held deep certifications with major vendors such as Cisco.

sections.heading: Below Range, Then BC Partners
sections.body: Presidio priced at $14 a share in March 2017, below its expected range. The stock traded in a narrow band in the years that followed. In 2019 BC Partners agreed to buy the company for about $2.1 billion, including debt. Presidio became private again. It kept running as an IT services provider for customers across the United States, with its headquarters in New York.

dek: Snapchat let young people talk in pictures that vanished, and its Stories format spread across the industry.
lede: Snap went public in 2017 and gave its new shareholders no voting rights at all. It was the largest tech offering since Alibaba. The company built Snapchat, the app that made photos vanish. Young people used it to talk in pictures instead of text, and rivals soon copied its Stories format. Snap called itself a camera company. It made its money selling ads between friends' posts.

sections.heading: Turning Down Facebook
sections.body: Evan Spiegel and Bobby Murphy started the app in 2011, while Spiegel was a student at Stanford. Its ghost logo hinted at messages that disappeared after viewing. The bet was that people wanted a place to share casual moments without a permanent record. That set Snapchat apart from Facebook. In 2013 Facebook offered to buy the company, and Spiegel turned it down.

sections.heading: Instagram Copies Stories
sections.body: Snap priced at $17 a share in March 2017 and jumped on its first day. The stock soon fell as Instagram copied Stories and user growth slowed. Snap rebuilt its Android app, invested in augmented reality and launched Spectacles glasses. The share price swung widely over the years. Its daily users later grew to several hundred million people. Snap remains public, led by its founders.

cover.artwork: Kohada Koheiji, from the series "One Hundred Ghost Tales (Hyaku monogatari)"

dek: Quantenna made the fast Wi-Fi chips inside the gateways and set-top boxes cable companies gave customers.
lede: Quantenna bet that Wi-Fi could carry high-definition video through the walls of a house and replace the cables. Its chipsets used many antennas at once to send more data and reach farther. Cable and telecom companies put them in the gateways and set-top boxes they handed to customers. When Quantenna filed to go public in 2016, video streaming was pushing home networks hard. Faster Wi-Fi had become a selling point.

sections.heading: A Stanford Professor's Antennas
sections.body: Behrooz Rezvani and Stanford professor Andrea Goldsmith founded Quantenna in 2006. Goldsmith was an expert in wireless theory. Early on, the company focused on an antenna method called MIMO, which uses several antennas at once. Quantenna shipped some of the first chips for each new Wi-Fi standard. Its chips reached homes inside the gear that service providers gave their customers.

sections.heading: Bought by ON Semiconductor
sections.body: Quantenna priced at $16 a share in October 2016. It grew with the arrival of faster Wi-Fi standards and won major service provider customers around the world, which used its chips in gateways and extenders. In 2019 ON Semiconductor bought Quantenna for about $1.07 billion in cash. The deal added Wi-Fi to ON's line of chips and gave it a foothold in home and enterprise wireless.

cover.theme: kites in the sky (signals through the air)
cover.artwork: Kites of Fukuroi and Distant View of Akiba in Totomi Province (Enshu Akiba enkei Fukuroi tako), from the series "One Hundred Famous Views in the Various Provinces (Shokoku meisho hyakkei)"

dek: The Trade Desk let ad buyers bid for space across websites, apps and streaming TV from one screen.
lede: The Trade Desk turned buying ads into something like trading stocks. Its software let agencies bid for ad space across thousands of websites, apps and video services in real time. Google and Facebook owned their own media. The Trade Desk owned none, so it pitched itself as a neutral tool that worked only for buyers. When it filed to go public in 2016, ad tech stocks had fallen out of favor after several weak offerings.

sections.heading: A Second Exchange Founder
sections.body: Jeff Green and Dave Pickles founded The Trade Desk in Ventura, California, in 2009. Green had already started AdECN, an ad exchange that Microsoft bought. The two saw online advertising turning into a market much like stock trading. They bet that buyers would want an independent platform that worked only for them, with no conflict from selling ads. Its customers became mostly ad agencies and large brands.

sections.heading: Profitable, Then Connected TV
sections.body: The Trade Desk priced at $18 a share in September 2016 and jumped on its first day. Unlike many ad tech peers, it was already profitable. The stock climbed for years as connected TV advertising grew. The company has stayed independent and kept its focus on serving ad buyers. It remains a public company led by Jeff Green, and its shares trade on Nasdaq.

dek: SecureWorks watched clients' networks around the clock and stepped in when attackers got through.
lede: SecureWorks was the first tech company to go public in 2016, and it priced below its target range. Its analysts watched other companies' networks around the clock, hunted for intruders and stepped in when attacks happened. Dell had bought the company in 2011 and sold only a small piece of it in the offering. Data breaches were front page news, but the tech offering market had nearly frozen.

sections.heading: A Threat Unit in Atlanta
sections.body: SecureWorks began in Atlanta in 1999. It sold security monitoring to banks and other firms that could not staff their own security teams. Its counter threat unit became known for research on hacking groups. The bet was that most companies would rather rent expert defenders than build their own teams in-house. Dell saw the business as a way to add security to its enterprise offerings.

sections.heading: Dell Lets Go to Sophos
sections.body: SecureWorks priced at $14 a share in April 2016, below its target range. Dell kept most of the shares and voting control, and it stayed the majority owner for the rest of SecureWorks' public life. The company later shifted toward its own extended detection and response software. In 2025 the British security firm Sophos completed its purchase of SecureWorks for about $859 million.

cover.artwork: A Warrior in Full Armor in a Grotto

dek: Canvas gave teachers and students one simple place online to post, turn in and grade coursework.
lede: Two graduate students at Brigham Young University built Canvas because the software schools used was clumsy and slow to improve. Teachers post assignments in it, and students turn them in. Universities and school districts use it to run courses, grade work and share materials. When Instructure filed to go public in 2015, Canvas was growing fast and winning campuses away from Blackboard, the long-time leader.

sections.heading: Open Source Out of BYU
sections.body: Brian Whitmer and Devlin Daley started Instructure in 2008 while they were graduate students at Brigham Young University. They believed the tools schools used were hard to use and slow to improve. Their bet was that a modern, open, cloud-based product would win over teachers and students first, and the schools would follow. Canvas launched in 2011, with an open source version alongside it.

sections.heading: Private, Public, Private Again
sections.body: Instructure priced at $16 a share in November 2015. Canvas kept adding schools, and the company also built a corporate training product. Thoma Bravo took Instructure private in 2020. It returned to the public market in 2021. In 2024 KKR bought the company for about $4.8 billion, and it went private again. Canvas remains one of the most widely used learning systems in American higher education.

dek: Rapid7 showed companies the weak spots in their systems and watched for attackers trying to use them.
lede: Rapid7 bought Metasploit, a widely used open source tool for testing security, and won a large following among researchers. Its own software scanned networks for weak spots, tested defenses and later watched for signs of an attack. When Rapid7 filed to go public in 2015, major breaches had pushed security to the top of company agendas. Companies had more systems to defend each year.

sections.heading: Buying Metasploit
sections.body: Rapid7 was founded in Boston in 2000 and began with vulnerability scanning. In 2009 it bought the Metasploit project, which brought it close to the community of security researchers. The bet was that defenders needed the same insight as attackers, delivered in software that IT teams could use every day. The company later moved its products to the cloud, where customers could run them without their own servers.

sections.heading: Subscriptions and AI Agents
sections.body: Rapid7 priced at $16 a share in July 2015 and rose on its first day. It expanded into detection and response and sold more of its products as cloud subscriptions. The company grew steadily, though profit came slowly. Corey Thomas led it as chief executive through most of its public years. Rapid7 remains public, based in Boston. In March 2026 it bought Kenzo Security, a startup that uses AI agents to investigate security alerts.

cover.artwork: Kakegawa: Crossing the Forty-eight Rapids on the Akiba Road (Kakegawa, Akiba michi shijuhachi segoe), no. 27 from the series "Famous Sights of the Fifty-three Stations (Gojusan tsugi meisho zue)," also known as the Vertical Tokaido

fate: Taken private by Vista Equity Partners, 2017 ($564M)
dek: Xactly worked out what salespeople were owed, so reps trusted their pay and managers knew which plans worked.
lede: Xactly existed because companies kept getting their salespeople's pay wrong. Many still tracked commissions in spreadsheets, which led to errors and disputes. Xactly's cloud software calculated pay automatically, showed reps their earnings and gave managers data on which plans worked. When it filed to go public in 2015, it was one of a wave of cloud companies that each sold to a single business department. Xactly's department was sales.

sections.heading: A Sales Leader's Grievance
sections.body: Christopher Cabrera founded Xactly in 2005 after years in sales leadership. He had seen how much time and trust companies lost to commission mistakes. His bet was that a cloud service could make pay accurate and clear. The data it gathered across many companies would then become valuable on its own. Xactly called this incentive compensation management and sold it to companies of many sizes.

sections.heading: Two Quiet Public Years
sections.body: Xactly priced at $8 a share in June 2015, below its expected range. The stock traded quietly for two years as the company grew. In 2017 Vista Equity Partners bought Xactly for about $564 million and took it private. It was one of several small public software firms Vista bought in that period. Xactly kept going as a private company focused on sales pay, planning and forecasting.

dek: TransUnion tracks how hundreds of millions of people borrow and repay, and sells that record to lenders.
lede: TransUnion started as the parent of a railcar leasing business. Today it keeps records of how people borrow and repay. Lenders use its credit reports to decide who gets a card, a car loan or a mortgage. It is one of three national credit bureaus in the United States, alongside Equifax and Experian. When TransUnion filed in 2015, private equity had owned it for years. It was returning to the public market as a data and analytics company.

sections.heading: A Chicago Credit Bureau
sections.body: TransUnion began in 1968 as a holding company for a railcar leasing business. A year later it bought a Chicago credit bureau, and credit grew into its main line of work. The bet was that credit files, gathered on a national scale and kept up to date, would become essential to lending. Computers made that possible. Over time TransUnion gathered files on hundreds of millions of people.

sections.heading: Fraud, Identity and Neustar
sections.body: TransUnion priced at $22.50 a share in June 2015. Advent and Goldman Sachs had bought it in 2012. As a public company it bought data firms, including Neustar in 2021, and expanded overseas. Its data now goes into fraud prevention, marketing and identity checks as well as lending. Like its rivals, it faces close scrutiny from regulators. TransUnion remains public, with headquarters in Chicago.

cover.artwork: Corner of Lake and La Salle Streets, Chicago, Marine Bank Building in the Year 1864

dek: Etsy gave knitters, potters and vintage sellers their own shops, and buyers a place to find them.
lede: Etsy went public as a certified B Corporation, a status almost no public company held. It ran a marketplace for things made by hand. Knitters, jewelers, potters and vintage sellers set up shops, and buyers came looking for items they could not find in big stores. The company stood out for its focus on its sellers and its social mission. It filed to go public in 2015, ten years after it started in Brooklyn.

sections.heading: A Craftsman Versus eBay
sections.body: Rob Kalin started Etsy in Brooklyn in 2005 with Chris Maguire and Haim Schoppik, and Jared Tarbell soon joined. Kalin was a craftsman, and he saw that eBay served makers poorly. His bet was that handmade goods deserved their own market, with a warmer feel and lower fees. Etsy grew slowly at first. Then millions of sellers joined, and it grew fast.

sections.heading: Face Masks, Then the NYSE
sections.body: Etsy priced at $16 a share in April 2015 and jumped on its first day. The stock then fell as growth slowed and new leaders cut costs. Josh Silverman led much of the turnaround. Etsy later dropped its B Corp status. Sales boomed in 2020 when sellers made face masks during the pandemic. In October 2025 Etsy moved its stock listing from Nasdaq to the New York Stock Exchange.

cover.theme: a woman at the spinning wheel (handcraft)

tagline: Super Bowl Ads and Domain Names
dek: GoDaddy sold millions of small businesses their web address, then the hosting, email and site tools to use it.
lede: For years GoDaddy was better known for loud Super Bowl ads than for anything it sold. What it sold was the internet's addresses. Millions of small businesses bought their domain names there, then added hosting, email and website tools. When GoDaddy filed to go public in 2015, a new leadership team under Blake Irving was trying to change that image. It wanted the company known for serving small business owners.

sections.heading: Jomax Becomes GoDaddy
sections.body: Bob Parsons started the company in 1997 as Jomax Technologies, after he sold his accounting software business. He renamed it GoDaddy in 1999, partly because the name was easy to remember. The bet was that the growing web would need cheap, simple domain names and hosting for everyone. Bold marketing, low prices and support around the clock made GoDaddy the biggest registrar.

sections.heading: The Second Try Works
sections.body: GoDaddy priced at $20 a share in April 2015. Years earlier it had withdrawn an attempt to go public. KKR, Silver Lake and other investors bought control in 2011. As a public company GoDaddy dropped its old ad style and built more software for small businesses. It later bought several hosting businesses abroad. GoDaddy remains public on the New York Stock Exchange.

cover.theme: gods playing a game of Go
cover.artwork: Wind and Thunder God Playing Go

dek: Box let big companies keep their files in the cloud without scaring their security teams.
lede: Box was famous for two things when it filed to go public in 2014: heavy spending on sales and growing losses. The offering was delayed into 2015. The product moved company files to the cloud. It offered storage and sharing like consumer services, plus the security, permissions and audit trails that large firms needed. Its customers included banks, drug makers and government agencies.

sections.heading: College Kids and Mark Cuban
sections.body: Aaron Levie and Dylan Smith started Box in 2005 while in college, with help from friends Jeff Queisser and Sam Ghods. Dallas billionaire Mark Cuban was an early investor. The company first targeted consumers, then shifted to businesses. Its bet was that companies would trust the cloud with sensitive files if a vendor made it safe and simple. Levie became chief executive.

sections.heading: Surviving an Activist
sections.body: Box priced at $14 a share in January 2015 and jumped on its first day. Then it worked for years to cut losses and turn a profit. In 2021 it survived a challenge from an activist investor, and it later added AI features. Its customers include many of the largest companies in the world. Box remains a public company led by Aaron Levie.

dek: OnDeck lent small businesses money online, with an answer in minutes and the cash within a day.
lede: OnDeck could size up a small business from its bank account and lend it money within a day. An owner applied online in minutes instead of sitting through a long bank process. OnDeck judged credit with data from bank accounts, sales and payments. When it filed to go public in late 2014, online lending was a hot topic. OnDeck was one of the first such lenders to reach the public market.

sections.heading: Cash Flow Over Paperwork
sections.body: Mitch Jacobs founded OnDeck in New York in 2006. He had run small businesses himself and found that banks often ignored them. His bet was that a business's daily cash flow said more about its credit than old-fashioned paperwork. OnDeck built its own scoring system and grew through brokers and partnerships with banks. Its loans were often short term, repaid daily or weekly.

sections.heading: Sold for $90 Million
sections.body: OnDeck priced at $20 a share in December 2014 and rose on its first day. Then the stock fell for years as funding costs and loan losses began to matter more than growth. The 2020 pandemic hit small businesses hard. Later that year Enova International bought OnDeck for about $90 million, far below its debut value. OnDeck continued as a brand inside Enova.

dek: Connecture let insurers and state exchanges show health plans online, so shoppers could compare prices and enroll.
lede: Connecture filed to go public in 2014, at the end of the first full enrollment season under the Affordable Care Act. The law had just opened public exchanges, and shopping for health insurance online was growing fast. Insurers, brokers and state exchanges used Connecture's software to show plans, compare prices and enroll customers. The company had spent years building those tools, and it saw a much larger role ahead.

sections.heading: Health Reform Opens a Door
sections.body: Connecture was based in the Milwaukee area. It spent years building quoting and enrollment software for health insurers. Then health reform pushed more people to shop for their own coverage. The company bet that buying a plan would become a retail experience, and that insurers and exchanges would need software to support it. It sold that software to insurers across the country.

sections.heading: Customers Leave, Francisco Arrives
sections.body: Connecture priced at $8 a share in December 2014, below its target range. The stock fell as some large customers left and losses grew. Francisco Partners invested in the company in 2016. In 2017 it agreed to take Connecture private for a small fraction of its offering value, and the deal closed in early 2018. The stock had traded on Nasdaq for about three years.

cover.theme: Waterloo Bridge in fog (a bridge to coverage)

dek: LendingClub let ordinary investors fund other people's personal loans online, often loans to pay off credit cards.
lede: LendingClub launched as an app on Facebook and ended up owning a bank. In between, it let ordinary people lend to each other. Borrowers applied online for personal loans, often to pay off credit cards, and investors funded those loans in small pieces. LendingClub earned fees in the middle. When it filed to go public in 2014, it was the largest such marketplace in the United States and a symbol of fintech's promise to bypass banks.

sections.heading: Cutting Out the Middle
sections.body: Renaud Laplanche founded LendingClub in 2006. It first launched as an app on Facebook. Laplanche believed banks charged too much on credit cards and paid savers too little. His bet was that an online marketplace could cut out the middle and give both sides a better deal. It grew quickly. Over time large institutions became the main investors on the platform.

sections.heading: A Scandal, Then a Bank
sections.body: LendingClub priced at $15 a share in December 2014 and jumped on its first day. In 2016 a scandal over loan sales forced Laplanche to resign, and the stock fell hard. Scott Sanborn took over as chief executive. In 2021 the company bought Radius Bank and became a bank itself, so it could hold loans and take deposits. LendingClub remains a public company.

cover.artwork: The actor Arashi Ryuzo II as Ishibe no Kinkichi, the moneylender

dek: Wayfair sold furniture and home goods online from a huge catalog, shipped mostly from suppliers' warehouses.
lede: Wayfair began as hundreds of small websites selling things like racks and bar stools. By 2014 it was one online store with millions of products, from sofas to light fixtures, most shipped straight from suppliers. People had long doubted that customers would buy bulky furniture without seeing it. When Wayfair filed to go public that year, its sales were growing fast. It was also spending heavily on advertising and losing money.

sections.heading: CSN Stores Becomes Wayfair
sections.body: Niraj Shah and Steve Conine started the business in 2002 as CSN Stores. They ran hundreds of small websites, each selling a narrow kind of product. In 2011 they merged the sites under the Wayfair name. Their bet was that one giant online store for the home could beat furniture showrooms on choice and price. Suppliers would hold the stock and ship it.

sections.heading: Boom Years and Real Stores
sections.body: Wayfair priced at $29 a share in October 2014 and rose on its first day. It built its own delivery network for large items. Sales soared during the 2020 pandemic as people fixed up their homes, then fell back. The company cut staff and opened its first large physical stores. Wayfair remains a public company led by its founders, with Niraj Shah as chief executive.

fate: Acquired by Just Eat Takeaway, 2021 ($7.3B); sold to Wonder, 2024
dek: Grubhub let hungry people order takeout from local restaurants online, without hunting for a paper menu.
lede: Grubhub started because Matt Maloney was tired of hunting for paper takeout menus. It put restaurant menus online. Diners searched nearby restaurants, then ordered and paid on the web or an app, and at first the restaurant handled delivery. Grubhub earned a commission on each order. When it filed to go public in 2014, it had just merged with Seamless, its New York rival. It was the leading online food ordering service in the United States.

sections.heading: Chicago Meets Seamless
sections.body: Matt Maloney and Mike Evans started Grubhub in Chicago in 2004. Their bet was that an online directory of menus with easy ordering would become the default way to get takeout. Grubhub would route hungry people to restaurants and take a commission, while the restaurants did the cooking and delivery. In 2013 it merged with Seamless, which joined the strongest positions in New York and Chicago. The company kept its headquarters in Chicago.

sections.heading: DoorDash Brings Couriers
sections.body: Grubhub priced at $26 a share in April 2014 and rose on its first day. Then rivals such as DoorDash and Uber Eats raced in with their own couriers, and Grubhub lost share. In 2021 Just Eat Takeaway bought the company for about $7.3 billion. Three years later it sold Grubhub to Wonder at a far lower value. Wonder kept the Grubhub name.

dek: Everyday Health gave readers health advice online and gave drug makers a way to reach patients and doctors.
lede: Everyday Health shelved its first attempt to go public in 2011 and came back three years later. By then it ran a network of health websites and apps for consumers and doctors. Readers came for advice on diet, illness and medicine. Pharmaceutical companies paid to reach them. The company also partnered with well-known names in health media. When it filed again in 2014, health information online was becoming big business.

sections.heading: It Started as Waterfront Media
sections.body: Ben Wolin and Mike Keriakos founded the business in 2002 as Waterfront Media. Its early hits included online diet programs. Over time it bought and built sites into a large health network and renamed itself Everyday Health. The bet was that health content and tools could draw a big audience. Drug makers would then pay to reach both patients and doctors.

sections.heading: Two Years, Then j2
sections.body: Everyday Health priced at $14 a share in March 2014. It added more services for doctors and grew revenue, but the stock stayed near its offering price. In 2016 j2 Global, now Ziff Davis, bought the company for about $465 million. Everyday Health became a core part of its digital media group. Its sites kept publishing under the Everyday Health name.

fate: Renamed Quotient; acquired by Neptune Retail Solutions, 2023
dek: Coupons.com gave shoppers digital discounts from big brands, online and on grocery store loyalty cards.
lede: Coupons.com was one of the oldest consumer internet companies still growing when it filed to go public in 2014. It had survived the dot-com crash by moving the Sunday coupon onto the web. Shoppers printed discounts or loaded them from its site and partner retailers, and consumer brands paid for each coupon redeemed. Later it put digital promotions onto grocery store loyalty cards. Its debut drew strong demand.

sections.heading: Aiming Offers at Shoppers
sections.body: Steven Boal founded the company in 1998. Many households already clipped coupons each week. Boal saw that the paper coupon business was huge but wasteful, and that the internet could aim offers at the right shoppers. The company survived the dot-com crash and built partnerships with major brands and grocery chains. The bet was that promotions would become digital, measurable and personal.

sections.heading: Quotient, Then Neptune
sections.body: Coupons.com priced at $16 a share in March 2014 and soared on its first day. The stock then fell back as growth slowed. In 2015 the company renamed itself Quotient Technology to reflect its wider promotions business, which ran through major grocery chains. Steven Boal led it for most of its public life. In 2023 Neptune Retail Solutions bought Quotient and took it private.

dek: Veeva built cloud software for drug makers alone, covering sales calls, clinical trials and regulatory work.
lede: Veeva was already profitable when it filed to go public in 2013, a rare thing for a young cloud company. It sold software to one industry: life sciences. Its first product, built on top of Salesforce, tracked drug company sales reps' visits to doctors. Then Veeva built its own platform for clinical, quality and regulatory content. It had needed only a small amount of outside capital to get there.

sections.heading: A Salesforce Veteran Narrows In
sections.body: Peter Gassner, a former Salesforce executive, and Matt Wallach founded Veeva in 2007. They believed a narrow industry focus would let them build deeper products than general software vendors could. Their bet was that pharmaceutical companies would pay well for software that fit their regulated world. Veeva used only a small amount of outside capital. It kept that single-industry focus.

sections.heading: Leaving Salesforce Behind
sections.body: Veeva priced at $20 a share in October 2013 and jumped on its first day. It kept growing and stayed profitable. In 2021 it became a public benefit corporation, one of the first large public companies to do so. Veeva later moved its customer software off Salesforce and onto its own platform. Peter Gassner remains chief executive, and Veeva remains public.

dek: RingCentral let businesses run their phone system from the cloud for a monthly fee, with no hardware.
lede: RingCentral started out offering online fax and phone features to small offices. The bigger bet was a whole office phone system that ran over the internet. Instead of buying hardware, a business paid a monthly fee for phone numbers, extensions and voicemail that worked on desk phones, computers and smartphones. When RingCentral filed to go public in 2013, small and midsize companies were moving to cloud services. Phone systems were next.

sections.heading: Two Vlads in Belmont
sections.body: Vlad Shmunis and Vlad Vendrow started RingCentral in 1999, with headquarters in Belmont, California. Their early service offered online fax and phone features for small offices. The bet was that a full phone system could run over the internet, with no switches or wiring anywhere in the office. The company grew steadily through the 2000s and moved toward larger customers.

sections.heading: Telecom Partners and Remote Work
sections.body: RingCentral priced at $13 a share in September 2013 and rose on its first day. It grew quickly and formed partnerships with large telecom companies to reach more customers. It also added messaging, video and contact center software. The stock soared in 2020 as remote work spread, then fell back. Founder Vlad Shmunis stepped down as chief executive in 2023. RingCentral remains a public company.

cover.theme: a temple bell at evening (the ring)

dek: Rocket Fuel used machine learning to decide, in real time, which online ads to buy for advertisers.
lede: Rocket Fuel nearly doubled on its first day of trading, and investors who bought at the offering later lost most of their money. The company used software to buy online ads. Its systems weighed many signals about each ad slot and decided in real time whether to bid. Advertisers paid it to run campaigns that hit their goals. When it filed to go public in 2013, automated ad buying was growing fast, and so was Rocket Fuel.

sections.heading: Yahoo Alumni and Algorithms
sections.body: George John, Richard Frankel and Abhinav Gupta founded Rocket Fuel in 2008. Several of the founders had worked at Yahoo. They believed artificial intelligence could buy ads far more efficiently than people working by hand. Their bet was that better algorithms would win the most valuable ad spending. A rocket theme ran through the company's offices and brand. It grew fast.

sections.heading: Sold to Sizmek
sections.body: Rocket Fuel priced at $29 a share in September 2013 and nearly doubled on its first day. Over the next few years the stock fell as competition grew and margins shrank. Its 2014 purchase of [x+1] added debt and complexity. In 2017 Sizmek bought Rocket Fuel for about $145 million, and offering-day buyers were left with a small part of what they paid. Sizmek itself filed for bankruptcy in 2019.

cover.artwork: Fireworks at Ryogoku (Ryogoku hanabi), from the series "Reflections on Water at Famous Places in Edo (Edo meisho mizu no omokage)"

dek: CDW sells computers, software and IT services to businesses, schools, hospitals and governments without big IT staffs.
lede: CDW started with Michael Krasny selling used computers through classified ads from his kitchen. The name stood for Computer Discount Warehouse. By 2013 a company, school or hospital could buy laptops, servers, software licenses and networking gear from CDW, often with setup and support included. Its account managers acted as trusted buyers for customers without big IT staffs. When CDW filed that year, it was returning to the public market after a 2007 leveraged buyout.

sections.heading: Computer Discount Warehouse
sections.body: Michael Krasny started CDW in 1984. He sold used computers through classified ads, working from his kitchen. He built a catalog and phone sales business that grew quickly in the 1990s. The bet was that businesses wanted one reliable place to buy all their technology, with expert advice and fast delivery. Krasny led the company for many years. Its customers came to include businesses of every size.

sections.heading: Paying Down the Buyout Debt
sections.body: CDW priced at $17 a share in June 2013. Madison Dearborn and Providence Equity had bought the company in 2007 and loaded it with debt. As a public company CDW paid down that debt and grew through cloud, security and services. It became a steady performer among tech stocks and has paid a dividend since 2013. Its headquarters later moved to Lincolnshire, Illinois. CDW remains public.

cover.artwork: Old Fashioned Brakeman on Freight Train

tagline: Cell Towers Aimed at the Sky
dek: Gogo let airline passengers get online in the air, then turned to serving private and business jets.
lede: Gogo built a network of cell towers on the ground that talked to airplanes overhead. Passengers on U.S. flights could pay for Wi-Fi in the air. Airlines installed the gear, and Gogo shared revenue with them. When Gogo filed to go public in 2013, it led in-flight internet, and getting online in the air was still a novelty for many travelers. Satellite rivals, though, promised faster service.

sections.heading: Aircell Wins the Airwaves
sections.body: Gogo began in 1991 as Aircell, which made phones for private planes. In 2006 it won the auction for air-to-ground radio spectrum. That let it build its own network for commercial jets across the continental United States. The bet was that travelers would pay to stay online in the air. Gogo launched its service in 2008 on American Airlines flights.

sections.heading: Back to Private Jets
sections.body: Gogo priced at $17 a share in June 2013. The stock rose, then fell as airlines moved to satellite service. In 2020 Gogo sold its commercial airline business to Intelsat and focused on business aviation. It moved its headquarters to Colorado. In 2024 it bought Satcom Direct to add satellite service for business jets. Gogo remains public and serves private jets.

cover.theme: a crane in flight over the waves

dek: KAYAK let travelers compare flights, hotels and rental cars from hundreds of booking sites in one search.
lede: KAYAK filed to go public in late 2010, then waited until 2012 to list. A few months after it finally did, Priceline agreed to buy it. The product searched travel sites so travelers did not have to. A single query showed flights, hotels and rental cars from airlines, booking sites and hotel chains side by side. KAYAK earned money from ads and when users clicked through to book. It was one of the best known travel brands online.

sections.heading: Staying Out of Booking
sections.body: Steve Hafner and Paul English founded KAYAK in 2004. Both had earlier worked on travel and consumer sites. They believed travel shopping was too slow and scattered, and that clean, fast search would win. Their bet was to stay a search engine and leave the booking to others, which kept KAYAK neutral among sellers. Its clean design drew many loyal users.

sections.heading: Public for a Few Months
sections.body: KAYAK priced at $26 a share in July 2012 and rose on its first day. Only a few months later, Priceline agreed to buy the company for about $1.8 billion. The deal closed in 2013. KAYAK continued as a separate brand inside Priceline, now Booking Holdings. Steve Hafner stayed on to lead it for years after the sale. Travelers still use KAYAK to compare prices.

cover.artwork: A Fisherman Drinking Beside His Canoe

dek: ServiceNow gave companies one cloud platform to track IT fixes, then HR, customer service and security work.
lede: ServiceNow began as a cloud help desk for IT tickets and grew into one of the largest software makers in the world. When something broke, an employee filed a ticket in its software, and IT staff tracked the fix. The company sold this as a subscription on a platform customers could extend. When ServiceNow filed to go public in 2012, large companies were starting to trust cloud software with core work. Frank Slootman was chief executive.

sections.heading: Glidesoft in San Diego
sections.body: Fred Luddy founded the company in San Diego in 2004 as Glidesoft. He had been chief technology officer at Peregrine Systems, a maker of IT management software. He wanted a platform that made it easy to build business workflows. His bet was that IT service management made a good first use, and that the same platform could later handle much more of a company's work.

sections.heading: Far Beyond IT
sections.body: ServiceNow priced at $18 a share in June 2012 and rose on its first day. It grew far beyond IT, into human resources, customer service and security work. Its value climbed into the hundreds of billions of dollars. Later chief executive Bill McDermott pushed it further into AI. ServiceNow remains a public company and one of the largest software makers in the world.

fate: Still public as Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META)
dek: Facebook connected people with their real friends and family online, and later bought Instagram and WhatsApp.
lede: Facebook's public offering was one of the most anticipated in history, and Nasdaq's systems stumbled on the first day. It was also one of the largest offerings ever, valuing the company at more than $100 billion. By 2012 about 900 million people used Facebook to share photos, news and messages with friends, and the News Feed kept them coming back. The company was moving fast to make money from mobile ads.

sections.heading: A Harvard Dorm Room
sections.body: Mark Zuckerberg launched the site from his Harvard dorm room in 2004 with roommates and classmates. It spread to other colleges, and in 2006 it opened to everyone. Zuckerberg turned down offers to sell. His bet was that real identity and real friends would make a social network more valuable than anonymous ones. That idea won Facebook a huge, loyal audience.

sections.heading: Glitches at Nasdaq
sections.body: Facebook priced at $38 a share in May 2012. Technical glitches at Nasdaq marred the first day, and the stock barely held its price. Shares fell by about half that year. Then Facebook bought Instagram and WhatsApp and moved to mobile ads, and growth took off. In 2021 it renamed itself Meta Platforms. Mark Zuckerberg still leads the company, and its users now number in the billions.

fate: Taken private by Vista Equity Partners, 2016 ($1.6B)
dek: Infoblox made the boxes and software that give every device on a network its address and name.
lede: Many companies still tracked their network addresses in spreadsheets when Infoblox filed to go public in 2012. Infoblox sold them a better way. Every device on a network needs an address, and every name like a web address needs to be turned into a number. Infoblox's appliances and software handled those jobs, known as DNS, DHCP and IP address management. Networks were growing more complex each year, with more devices to track.

sections.heading: A Box for Network Basics
sections.body: Stuart Bailey founded Infoblox in Chicago in 1999. He saw that these basic network services were usually built from free software and maintained by hand. His bet was that a dedicated appliance would make them easier to run and more reliable. The company later moved its headquarters to Silicon Valley. Its customers included large enterprises, service providers and government agencies.

sections.heading: DNS Turns to Security
sections.body: Infoblox priced at $16 a share in April 2012 and rose on its first day. It added security products built on its knowledge of DNS, and those tools became a growing part of the business. Growth slowed in later years. In 2016 Vista Equity Partners bought the company for about $1.6 billion and took it private. Infoblox continues as a private company focused on networking and security.

dek: Proofpoint kept spam, phishing and malware out of company inboxes, and kept sensitive data from leaking out.
lede: Proofpoint's founder had been the chief technology officer at Netscape, and he started the company while spam was flooding inboxes. Proofpoint protected corporate email. Its software screened messages for spam, phishing and malware, and kept sensitive data from leaking out. Email was the most common way attackers reached employees. When Proofpoint filed to go public in 2012, it was moving its products to the cloud and adding archiving and compliance tools.

sections.heading: Betting Email Would Last
sections.body: Eric Hahn founded Proofpoint in 2002. Spam was flooding inboxes, and companies needed a better filter. Gary Steele became chief executive in the company's first year and led it for many years. The bet was that email would stay at the center of business. Attacks against it would keep getting more targeted and more costly. Phishing attacks were already growing more common.

sections.heading: A $12.3 Billion Buyout
sections.body: Proofpoint priced at $13 a share in April 2012. It grew steadily as phishing became the main way into companies, and it bought several smaller security firms along the way. The stock rose for years. In 2021 Thoma Bravo bought Proofpoint for about $12.3 billion, one of the largest software buyouts of that period. Under private ownership Proofpoint kept buying companies and widening its products.

cover.artwork: Woman Reading a Letter, from the series Ten Classes of Women's Physiognomy (Fujo ninso juppon) (Fumi yomu onna)

dek: CafePress let anyone sell T-shirts, mugs and posters with their own designs, printed only when ordered.
lede: CafePress let anyone open a shop without owning a single T-shirt. A user uploaded art, and CafePress printed the shirt, mug or poster only when someone ordered it. Sellers carried no inventory. The site hosted millions of small shops and became known for gifts, slogans and fan merchandise. When it filed to go public in 2012, it was one of the earliest print on demand companies, thirteen years old.

sections.heading: Printing in Kentucky
sections.body: Fred Durham and Maheesh Jain founded CafePress in 1999. They saw that digital printing could make single items cheaply. Their bet was that people would pay a premium for custom products, and that a marketplace of designers would fill the catalog. Shop owners earned a share of each sale. The company grew through the 2000s and moved much of its production to Kentucky.

sections.heading: Etsy and Zazzle Close In
sections.body: CafePress priced at $19 a share in March 2012. Its stock fell soon after as competition from sites like Etsy and Zazzle grew. The company sold off several businesses to focus on its core. Many shop owners moved to other print on demand sites. In 2018 Snapfish bought CafePress for about $25 million and kept it selling custom products online.

dek: Millennial Media placed ads for brands inside phone apps and mobile websites, using data to target users.
lede: Millennial Media started selling ads on phones in Baltimore in 2006, before the iPhone existed. It connected advertisers with apps and mobile websites and used data to reach the right users. Smartphones were spreading fast, but advertisers had only begun to move their budgets to mobile. When it filed to go public in 2012, Millennial was one of the largest independent mobile ad networks. Its rivals were Google and Apple.

sections.heading: Betting on the Phone Early
sections.body: Paul Palmieri co-founded Millennial Media in Baltimore in 2006, before the iPhone. The company bet that the phone would become a major ad medium, and that an independent network could gather enough apps to matter. It built tools that let app developers place ads inside their apps. Millennial grew as smartphones spread and app makers looked for ways to earn money.

sections.heading: Folded Into AOL
sections.body: Millennial Media priced at $13 a share in March 2012 and jumped on its first day. Competition from Facebook and Google soon squeezed its business. It bought Jumptap in 2013 to add scale. In 2015 AOL bought Millennial Media for about $238 million. AOL, then owned by Verizon, folded it into its own advertising business, and the Millennial Media name faded soon after.

dek: Demandware ran the online stores of big retail and consumer brands from the cloud, for a cut of sales.
lede: Demandware charged retailers a share of every sale that passed through the online stores it ran for them. It did well only when they did. Big brands used its cloud software to build sites, manage products and process orders without running their own servers. When Demandware filed to go public in 2012, many retailers still ran older e-commerce software in their own data centers. Online shopping was growing quickly.

sections.heading: Intershop's Founder Tries Again
sections.body: Stephan Schambach founded Demandware near Boston in 2004. He had earlier founded Intershop, a German e-commerce software company. His bet was that retailers would rather rent a fully managed store in the cloud than build and maintain their own systems. Tying fees to customer sales lined Demandware up with the retailers it served. Its customers included apparel, footwear and consumer brands.

sections.heading: Becoming Commerce Cloud
sections.body: Demandware priced at $16 a share in March 2012 and jumped on its first day. It grew as more retailers moved to the cloud. In 2016 Salesforce bought Demandware for about $2.8 billion, one of the largest deals Salesforce had made to that point. Demandware became Salesforce Commerce Cloud. Retailers kept using the platform under its new name, now part of the Salesforce product line.

dek: Yelp let people read and write reviews of local businesses, from restaurants and salons to plumbers.
lede: Yelp began as an email tool for asking friends for recommendations. Users liked writing reviews more, so reviews became the product. People rated restaurants, dentists, mechanics and more, and others read them before choosing where to go. Local businesses paid for ads and enhanced listings. When Yelp filed to go public in 2012, it had tens of millions of reviews, and smartphones made them easy to check on the spot. Its biggest rival was Google.

sections.heading: Two PayPal Alumni
sections.body: Jeremy Stoppelman and Russel Simmons founded Yelp in 2004. Both had worked at PayPal. Their first idea was an email system for asking friends for recommendations. Users liked writing reviews more, and the founders followed them. The bet was that honest reviews from ordinary people would become the main guide for local decisions. The site started in San Francisco and spread city by city.

sections.heading: Fighting Google Over Search
sections.body: Yelp priced at $15 a share in March 2012 and jumped on its first day. It kept growing as people searched for local businesses on their phones. Yelp fought with Google over search results and with businesses over its review filter. Its revenue came to rely on ads from local businesses and on services such as restaurant waitlists. Jeremy Stoppelman led it as chief executive, and Yelp remains public.

cover.artwork: The Habit of Criticizing Others (Ta o soshiru kuse), from the series "Seven Bad Habits (Nakute nana kuse)"

fate: Taken private by Marlin Equity Partners, 2018 ($521M)
dek: Bazaarvoice collected customer ratings and reviews and showed them on retail and brand websites.
lede: Bazaarvoice bought its main rival soon after going public, and the Justice Department sued to undo the deal. The company powered the reviews on other companies' websites. Retailers and brands used its software to collect ratings and comments and display them next to products. When Bazaarvoice filed to go public in 2012, it served many of the biggest retailers and brands. Online shoppers had come to expect reviews on product pages.

sections.heading: A Network of Shared Reviews
sections.body: Brett Hurt founded Bazaarvoice in Austin in 2005. He had earlier built an analytics company. He believed customer voices could sell products better than marketing copy. His bet was that every online store would need reviews, and that one shared network could serve them all. That network let brands share reviews with the retailers that sold their products. Reviews guided shoppers and gave companies feedback.

sections.heading: The PowerReviews Lawsuit
sections.body: Bazaarvoice priced at $12 a share in February 2012 and rose on its first day. Soon after, it bought PowerReviews, its main rival, and the Justice Department sued. A court ruled against the deal, and Bazaarvoice had to sell PowerReviews. In 2018 Marlin Equity Partners bought the company for about $521 million. Bazaarvoice continues as a private company in Austin.

cover.theme: a busy street in Cairo (the bazaar)

fate: Taken private by Centre Lane Partners, 2021
dek: Synacor built the home pages, email and logins that cable and internet companies gave customers under their own brands.
lede: Synacor was one of the few tech companies of its size based in Buffalo, New York, and its work carried other companies' names. Cable and telecom firms used its software for their customer home pages, email and logins. Subscribers saw their provider's brand. Synacor made money from ads and search on those pages. It was a quiet business, and it filed to go public in 2012, fourteen years after its founding.

sections.heading: Partner Instead of Build
sections.body: Synacor was founded in Buffalo in 1998. It grew by serving internet providers that wanted their own branded portals without building them. Its early customers included regional cable and telecom firms. The bet was that these companies would rather partner than build, and that the portals would draw enough users to earn steady ad revenue. Synacor also offered login tools that let subscribers reach online video.

sections.heading: Buying Zimbra
sections.body: Synacor priced at $5 a share in February 2012. It later bought Zimbra email software to widen its products, and many providers around the world came to use that email platform. Revenue fell as customers changed their portal strategies. In 2021 Centre Lane Partners bought Synacor and took it private, ending nine years as a public company. Synacor continued to serve internet providers.

cover.artwork: Head of a Buffalo, from Die Zweite Thierfolge

dek: Zynga made free social games like FarmVille and Zynga Poker, then became a major mobile game publisher.
lede: Zynga was named after Mark Pincus's bulldog, and its games once filled Facebook. FarmVille and Zynga Poker drew tens of millions of players, who invited their friends to join. Most games were free. The money came from players buying virtual goods. When it filed to go public in 2011, Zynga was the largest social game maker in the world, in a category that was still new.

sections.heading: Games That Spread Through Friends
sections.body: Mark Pincus founded Zynga in San Francisco in 2007. He saw that Facebook's platform could spread games among friends quickly. His bet was that simple, free games played in short sessions would attract a mass audience, and that a small share of players would pay for extras. Zynga Poker was one of its first big hits on Facebook. FarmVille followed in 2009.

sections.heading: From Facebook to Phones
sections.body: Zynga priced at $10 a share in December 2011 and fell below that on its first day. Facebook changed its rules and players moved to phones, and Zynga struggled. It rebuilt itself as a mobile game publisher through acquisitions, and its mobile hits included Words With Friends. In 2022 Take-Two Interactive bought Zynga for about $12.7 billion. Take-Two kept Zynga as its mobile games label.
